c01.display: Welcome back to NLP, Simply Explained. This is unit 1, lesson 3: text classification.
c01.spoken: Welcome back to N L P, Simply Explained. This is unit 1, lesson 3: text classification.

c02.display: Last time we cut text into tokens. Today we use those pieces to answer a simple question about a whole message: which kind is it?
c02.spoken: Last time we cut text into tokens. Today we use those pieces to answer a simple question about a whole message: which kind is it?

c03.display: Here is the idea in one line. Classification means putting each piece of text into the right box.
c03.spoken: Here is the idea in one line. Classification means putting each piece of text into the right box.

c04.display: You use text classifiers every day, often without noticing. Here are four.
c04.spoken: You use text classifiers every day, often without noticing. Here are four.

c05.display: Your email decides whether each message is spam or not spam.
c05.spoken: Your email decides whether each message is spam or not spam.

c06.display: Shopping sites sort reviews into positive and negative.
c06.spoken: Shopping sites sort reviews into positive and negative.

c07.display: Help desks route each support ticket to the team that should answer it.
c07.spoken: Help desks route each support ticket to the team that should answer it.

c08.display: And your phone guesses which language a message is written in, so it can offer to translate it.
c08.spoken: And your phone guesses which language a message is written in, so it can offer to translate it.

c09.display: The program doing the sorting is called a classifier. It reads a piece of text and picks one label from a fixed list.
c09.spoken: The program doing the sorting is called a classifier. It reads a piece of text and picks one label from a fixed list.

c10.display: For example, it reads "WIN a FREE prize!!!" and picks the label "spam".
c10.spoken: For example, it reads "WIN a FREE prize!!!" and picks the label "spam".

c11.display: Think of a post-office sorter: every letter goes into exactly one pigeonhole, based on what's written on it.
c11.spoken: Think of a post-office sorter: every letter goes into exactly one pigeonhole, based on what's written on it.

c12.display: Nobody writes the sorting rules by hand. A classifier learns them from examples, in four steps.
c12.spoken: Nobody writes the sorting rules by hand. A classifier learns them from examples, in four steps.

c13.display: Collect: gather lots of texts that already have the right label, like emails people have marked as spam or not spam.
c13.spoken: Collect: gather lots of texts that already have the right label, like emails people have marked as spam or not spam.

c14.display: Find clues: turn each text into clues the computer can count. The simplest clues are the words themselves.
c14.spoken: Find clues: turn each text into clues the computer can count. The simplest clues are the words themselves.

c15.display: Train: let the computer learn which clues usually point to which label.
c15.spoken: Train: let the computer learn which clues usually point to which label.

c16.display: Predict: give it a new text it has never seen, and it picks a label.
c16.spoken: Predict: give it a new text it has never seen, and it picks a label.

c17.display: Here is a small made-up example. Out of a hundred training emails, this table shows how many spam and normal emails contain each word.
c17.spoken: Here is a small made-up example. Out of a hundred training emails, this table shows how many spam and normal emails contain each word.

c18.display: "free" appears in thirty spam emails, but only two normal ones. A strong hint of spam.
c18.spoken: "free" appears in thirty spam emails, but only two normal ones. A strong hint of spam.

c19.display: "winner" is similar: eighteen spam emails, just one normal one.
c19.spoken: "winner" is similar: eighteen spam emails, just one normal one.

c20.display: "meeting" goes the other way: it appears in twenty-five normal emails and only one spam email.
c20.spoken: "meeting" goes the other way: it appears in twenty-five normal emails and only one spam email.

c21.display: And "invoice" leans towards normal mail too, but more weakly: twelve normal, three spam.
c21.spoken: And "invoice" leans towards normal mail too, but more weakly: twelve normal, three spam.

c22.display: One of the oldest and simplest classifiers is called Naive Bayes. The idea is to let the clues vote.
c22.spoken: One of the oldest and simplest classifiers is called Naive Bayes. The idea is to let the clues vote.

c23.display: Every word in the email is a clue.
c23.spoken: Every word in the email is a clue.

c24.display: Words that are common in spam add weight to the spam side.
c24.spoken: Words that are common in spam add weight to the spam side.

c25.display: Words that are common in normal mail add weight to the normal side.
c25.spoken: Words that are common in normal mail add weight to the normal side.

c26.display: Whichever side ends up heavier wins. And it's called "naive" because it judges each word on its own, ignoring word order, which is a simplification that works surprisingly well.
c26.spoken: Whichever side ends up heavier wins. And it's called "naive" because it judges each word on its own, ignoring word order, which is a simplification that works surprisingly well.

c27.display: So how do we know if a spam filter is any good? There are two questions to ask, and they're easy to mix up.
c27.spoken: So how do we know if a spam filter is any good? There are two questions to ask, and they're easy to mix up.

c28.display: The first is precision: of all the mail the filter marked as spam, how much really was spam? Low precision means real emails go missing.
c28.spoken: The first is precision: of all the mail the filter marked as spam, how much really was spam? Low precision means real emails go missing.

c29.display: The second is recall: of all the spam that arrived, how much did the filter catch? Low recall means spam fills your inbox. A good filter needs both.
c29.spoken: The second is recall: of all the spam that arrived, how much did the filter catch? Low recall means spam fills your inbox. A good filter needs both.

c30.display: Let's check our filter on a hundred test emails.
c30.spoken: Let's check our filter on a hundred test emails.

c31.display: It marked twenty of them as spam.
c31.spoken: It marked twenty of them as spam.

c32.display: Eighteen of those twenty really were spam, so its precision is eighteen out of twenty: ninety percent.
c32.spoken: Eighteen of those twenty really were spam, so its precision is eighteen out of twenty: ninety percent.

c33.display: But the test set held twenty-four spam emails in total, and it caught eighteen. So its recall is eighteen out of twenty-four: seventy-five percent.
c33.spoken: But the test set held twenty-four spam emails in total, and it caught eighteen. So its recall is eighteen out of twenty-four: seventy-five percent.

c34.display: Time for a quick quiz. An important email from your boss lands in the spam folder. Which number went down: precision, or recall?
c34.spoken: Time for a quick quiz. An important email from your boss lands in the spam folder. Which number went down: precision, or recall?

c36.display: It's precision. A real email marked as spam is a false alarm, and false alarms lower precision.
c36.spoken: It's precision. A real email marked as spam is a false alarm, and false alarms lower precision.

c37.display: Let's recap. A classifier reads text and picks one label from a fixed list.
c37.spoken: Let's recap. A classifier reads text and picks one label from a fixed list.

c38.display: It learns from labelled examples, using words as clues.
c38.spoken: It learns from labelled examples, using words as clues.

c39.display: Naive Bayes lets every word vote on its own, and the heavier side wins.
c39.spoken: Naive Bayes lets every word vote on its own, and the heavier side wins.

c40.display: Precision asks: were the alarms right? Recall asks: did we miss anything?
c40.spoken: Precision asks: were the alarms right? Recall asks: did we miss anything?
